entry.title: pi-claude-bridge: your Claude Pro, Max or Team subscription inside pi
entry.summary: pi-claude-bridge wires pi to the Claude Code Agent SDK so you can use Opus, Sonnet and Haiku from your Pro, Max or Team subscription as regular pi models, with no API key and every tool call flowing through pi's TUI.
entry.content:
At work the model budget is a Claude Team account. And that always raises the same question: does this session come out of the subscription, or out of a separate API key? pi-claude-bridge goes exactly there: Claude models show up in pi's /model and the conversation spends subscription quota instead of billed tokens.

What it actually is¶

It's a pi extension built on the Claude Code Agent SDK. It started as a fork of Prateek Sunal's claude-agent-sdk-pi and does two things:

  1. Provider — Registers a claude-bridge provider with the Claude models from pi-ai's catalog. Every tool call flows through pi's TUI, so you see what you'd see with any other model.
  2. AskClaude tool — Lets you delegate a question to Claude Code while running another provider. It's marked deprecated.
pi install npm:pi-claude-bridge

Requires pi 1.2.0 or newer for all models to be available.

Using it as a provider¶

/model claude-bridge/claude-opus-5

That's it. Behind the scenes pi translates its tools into Claude Code's format, so the workflow doesn't change: same tools, same session, same subagents. A few things do change and are worth knowing:

  • Bash gets a 120-second timeout, Claude Code's default. pi's bash has no timeout of its own, so it inherits the bridge's.
  • Skills are forwarded into Claude Code's system prompt.
  • Mid-turn steering reaches Claude at the next tool boundary, not immediately.
  • The model list is pi-ai's. When pi-ai adds a Claude model it appears in /model after you update the package, without waiting for a bridge release. Dated snapshot ids (claude-opus-4-5-20251101) are hidden.

Login: the bridge has no login of its own¶

This is where quite a few people trip first (issue #201 in the repo). The extension does not authenticate against Anthropic on its own: it spawns the claude binary and uses whatever session Claude Code already has. pi's /login for the anthropic provider is unrelated, and using it expecting the bridge to inherit it ends with you paying Extra Usage without noticing.

So the first thing is to check which account claude is logged in with. Inside Claude Code:

/status

Account:       you@company.com
Organization:  Your Company
Login method:  Claude Team account

If it says Claude Max account, Claude Pro account or Claude Team account, the bridge uses that session. If it says an API key, it doesn't.

And just in case: turn Extra Usage off in Claude's settings. If Claude Code can't draw on your subscription for a request, the fallback is billing you the overage, and that's better found out before the invoice than after.

1M context¶

A million-token context isn't available the same way on every plan, and the bridge needs to know yours. It's configured in ~/.pi/agent/claude-bridge.json:

{
  "provider": {
    "plan": "max",
    "longContextExtraUsage": false
  }
}

With plan: "pro" (the default) you get 1M on Fable 5/5.1, Opus 5.5/5/4.8/4.7 and Sonnet 5.5/5. Opus 4.6 only reaches 1M on a Max plan or with Extra Usage, and Sonnet 4.6 only with Extra Usage. Watch the value's name: if your account is a company one, the README still tells you to set max, because that's what enables long context on Team Premium and Enterprise. Odd, but that's how it is. If your plan advertises 1M but Claude Code won't serve it, forceTwoHundredK pins specific models to 200K:

{
  "provider": {
    "plan": "max",
    "forceTwoHundredK": ["claude-opus-4-6"]
  }
}

The rest of the config¶

{
  "provider": {
    "strictMcpConfig": true,
    "autoMemoryEnabled": false,
    "pathToClaudeCodeExecutable": "/home/you/.nix-profile/bin/claude"
  },
  "askClaude": {
    "enabled": false,
    "defaultMode": "read",
    "allowFullMode": true
  }
}

strictMcpConfig is on by default and blocks MCP servers from ~/.claude.json and .mcp.json. That makes sense: if you already have MCP in pi, loading Claude Code's on top duplicates tools and burns context. Cloud MCP (Gmail, Drive via claude.ai OAuth) is always blocked.

pathToClaudeCodeExecutable is for when the SDK's bundled binaries can't run on your system. Nix is the classic case: point it at the claude from your profile.

What to know before using it¶

This is not just another provider, and it has traps the repo documents. The important ones:

Rebuilding a session re-sends the whole conversation. The bridge rewrites Claude Code's session from pi's history whenever the two diverge: after an abort, a /compact, tree navigation, an API error, or on returning to a session. The next request usually misses the prompt cache for everything past the system prompt. In abort-heavy sessions you feel it in the bill.

Files Claude Code edits don't survive a rebuild. The edit itself does, it stays in the history as a tool call and result. What's lost is the file snapshot after the edit. @file expansions are preserved.

System prompt changes mid-session may not reach the model. Claude Code records the first request's prompt (project context, skills, extension instructions) and reuses it on resume. That keeps the cached prefix stable, but if you edit AGENTS.md mid-session it may not take effect until a rebuild or compaction.

Exported ANTHROPIC_* variables hijack the child process. An ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN in your environment redirects Claude Code to that gateway and every turn fails with its auth error. If you have one of those in your .zshrc, drop it from the pi process.

modelOverrides from models.json doesn't work here. They only apply to pi-side settings like the compaction threshold. To change contextWindow you edit src/models.ts or use forceTwoHundredK.

Details that surprised me for the better¶

Claude Code hooks keep working. ~/.claude/settings.json fires inside bridge turns. That can be useful or a mess: a hook injecting Claude-specific guidance duplicates what your pi extensions already do. The escape hatch is the one the README suggests:

[ -n "$PI_CODING_AGENT" ] && exit 0

pi sets PI_CODING_AGENT=true on child processes, so the hook opts itself out when it runs inside pi.

Compaction is still pi's job. The bridge routes those calls to isolated Claude Code queries, leaving the live session untouched until pi finishes rewriting the history.

Plan usage can be read from other extensions. Claude Code emits a rate_limit_event when a usage window changes, and the bridge passes it through the after_provider_response event as anthropic-ratelimit-unified-* headers, with the same names the Anthropic API uses. An extension that already reads those headers for the native anthropic provider can accept claude-bridge unchanged.

Coexistence with subagents. With @gotgenes/pi-subagents you need this in ~/.pi/agent/subagents.json:

{"promptInheritance": {"claude-bridge": "portable"}}

On billing¶

Anthropic announced and then un-announced a change to how Agent SDK usage gets billed. As of today this extension spends your subscription quota just like Claude Code. There is also an announced change where Max and Team plans include monthly API credits, and the repo doesn't know yet whether that will eventually reach the bridge: the consensus in the issues is "same as ever for now".

That's why it interests me at work and not at home: where Claude is already paid for, the bridge makes sense; where it isn't, none.

How I use it¶

On the work machine I have a Claude Team account and pi is my harness. This is what I want to set up there, and it's worth saying plainly: I haven't tested it on that machine yet. What I have verified is what I describe above — configuration, how it works inside, and the traps the repo documents. Once it's been running for a few days I'll update this post with the verdict and with whatever plan value I end up with.

The approach is what interests me: the TUI is pi's, the tools are pi's, the skills are pi's, and underneath the thing talking to Anthropic is Claude Code with my session. No loose API keys, and no choosing between the agent I like and the model that's already paid for.

The real downside, when I test it, will be abort-heavy sessions, where the bridge pays the price of rebuilding history.

At home the setup is the opposite: an OpenCode Go subscription and pi-provider-opencode-console for a live model catalog.

Resources¶

  • pi-claude-bridge on GitHub — Code, config and known issues
  • On npm — pi install npm:pi-claude-bridge
  • Claude Agent SDK — The foundation it builds on
  • claude-agent-sdk-pi — The project it came from
  • The OpenCode bridge — The other provider extension I use

entry.title: pi-provider-opencode-console: live OpenCode Go models without waiting for pi releases
entry.summary: pi-provider-opencode-console adds OpenCode Console and OpenCode Go to pi with OAuth device-code login and a live model catalog, so you no longer wait for a pi release to refresh its static model list.
entry.content:
For my personal work I use the OpenCode Go subscription as the model provider in pi. And there was one detail that annoyed me every week: when OpenCode changed the subscription model catalog, pi kept showing me the old list until a new release shipped.

The problem: a model list frozen into the binary¶

pi does not discover models at runtime for its built-in providers. The catalog lives in pi-ai, in a file generated at build time:

// This file is auto-generated by scripts/generate-models.ts
// Do not edit manually - run 'npm run generate-models' to update

For a provider with a public API and a stable catalog that's fine. For a subscription that adds and retires models every few weeks, it's constant friction: you see new names on the OpenCode site that don't exist in /model, and retired models that are still there taking up space.

The alternative was hand-editing models.json, which is worse: you maintain it, it drifts, and model overrides don't always behave the same way with extension providers.

The fix: device-code OAuth and a live catalog¶

pi-provider-opencode-console is a pi extension that registers two new providers — opencode-console and opencode-go-console — with OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant login (RFC 8628) and model discovery against OpenCode's real catalog.

pi install npm:pi-provider-opencode-console

The two providers are deliberately distinct from the ones pi ships with:

Provider Auth Model catalog
opencode / opencode-go (built-in) API key Static, compiled into pi-ai
opencode-console / opencode-go-console (extension) OAuth device code Live, from the server

That leaves the built-in providers untouched and lets you pick whichever matches your setup: API key or subscription. No name collisions, no credential conflicts.

Login¶

The flow is the usual one: you request the login, pi gives you a code and a URL, you approve in the browser, done.

/login opencode-go-console

# pi prints a user code and the verification URL
# you approve in the browser and the credential lands in ~/.pi/agent/auth.json

For the full console (the one that absorbed Zen) it's the same flow:

/login opencode-console

Both share the device-code session, so authenticating one leaves the other ready. The credential is stored as oauth in auth.json, and the access token renews itself: with less than five minutes to expiry the extension refreshes before the next request, single-flight so two concurrent calls don't request two tokens, and mirrors the rotated token into the sibling entry.

One important thing: the extension is OAuth-only. It does not offer pi's generic "Enter API key" login. If you want API-key access with a static list, that's exactly why the built-in providers exist.

Where the models come from¶

Each provider has its own source:

  • opencode-go-console pulls the public GET https://opencode.ai/inference/go/v1/models catalog, the lite list, and enriches it with models.dev data while dropping disabled or deprecated ids.
  • opencode-console pulls the org-scoped GET {server}/api/config endpoint with Authorization: Bearer and x-org-id, so each organization sees the models it actually has.

To refresh without logging in again:

/opencode-go-console refresh

And to see what's behind it:

/opencode-go-console status    # auth method, account, org, token expiry
/opencode-go-console logout    # clears the Go credential, keeps Console's

The console provider also has switch-org to change organization when the session isn't already scoped to one from the browser. If the grant requested org scoping, switch-org doesn't apply: you log in again.

The detail that makes this work well¶

OpenCode does not expose every model over the same protocol. Some models speak anthropic-messages, others openai-completions, others openai-responses, and the Gemini ones go through google-generative-ai. The extension routes each request to the right wire API for the model you picked, and normalizes the base URL per API kind before letting the SDK compose its own:

API kind Normalized base
anthropic-messages /inference[/go]/anthropic
openai-completions /inference[/go]/openai/v1
openai-responses /inference[/go]/openai/v1
google-generative-ai /inference[/go]/google/v1beta

Streaming and parsing are delegated to pi-ai's implementations instead of being reimplemented. That means a new model speaking an already-supported protocol works without touching the extension, and streaming bugs get fixed where they belong: in pi-ai.

It also injects per-request identity headers (x-opencode-org-id, x-opencode-client, x-opencode-request), which is what makes the session recognizable as yours on OpenCode's side.

Configuration¶

Just two environment variables, and usually none:

Variable Default What for
OPENCODE_CONSOLE_SERVER https://opencode.ai/console Self-hosted consoles. Persisted to auth.json on first sign-in.
PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR ~/.pi/agent pi's agent directory. Useful for testing in an isolated setup.

Migrating from older versions¶

2.0 broke compatibility on purpose: service-key auth (sk-…) was removed. If you still have one of those entries in auth.json, it's inert and pi reports "Provider is not configured". Delete it and do the device-code sign-in.

# coming from 1.x? check and clean up
cat ~/.pi/agent/auth.json

How I use it¶

I run pi on two machines with two different budgets: the OpenCode Go subscription for personal work and the Claude subscription for work (that's pi-claude-bridge). On the personal machine, this extension removed an entire class of friction: there's no longer a "let's see if this week's release brings the new model" moment.

The catalog you see in /model is the one you're paying for right now. If OpenCode adds a model in the morning, I have it in pi after a refresh, without updating anything.

And if you want to know how each of those models performs before picking one, aa-opencode crosses the catalog with Artificial Analysis benchmarks.

Resources¶

  • pi-provider-opencode-console on GitHub — Code and docs
  • On npm — pi install npm:pi-provider-opencode-console
  • OpenCode Console — The console and model catalog
  • RFC 8628 — OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant
  • What is pi? — First part of the pi series

entry.title: aa-opencode: OpenCode models with benchmarks and price in one table
entry.summary: aa-opencode crosses the OpenCode model catalog with Artificial Analysis benchmarks and prints one table with intelligence, speed, and price per model. A Python CLI I just published.
entry.content:
I use OpenCode as one of the model providers in pi, and there's the problem: the list of available models is long and says nothing. You get names, sure. What you don't get is how well each one reasons, how fast it answers, or what a million tokens costs you. Picking by eye is a coin toss.

Artificial Analysis publishes exactly that: independent intelligence, coding, and math indices, plus output speed, time to first token, and price. But it has its own catalog and its own names, so crossing it by hand against OpenCode's models is a chunk of work every time you want to check.

So I wrote aa-opencode: it grabs the OpenCode model list, crosses it with the Artificial Analysis API, and prints a table. Nothing else. It's about 430 lines of Python with httpx and rich.

Installation¶

uv tool install git+https://github.com/pcaro/aa-opencode

It needs an Artificial Analysis API key, which is free: create an account, generate the key, and put it in the environment.

export ARTIFICIAL_ANALYSIS_API_KEY="your-key"

It also reads AA_API_KEY, and if you want to pass it ad hoc there's --api-key.

Usage¶

# Default table, sorted by intelligence
aa-opencode

# Other sort keys
aa-opencode --sort price
aa-opencode --sort speed
aa-opencode --sort coding

# JSON to chain into something else
aa-opencode --format json

By default it pulls the Go catalog. For the Zen catalog:

aa-opencode --catalog zen

What comes out¶

The Go catalog has 33 models with data in Artificial Analysis. The first thing that jumps out is that the smartest model in the catalog isn't the one I'd use for coding every day. gemini-4-argon-contributor leads with a 52.6 index and costs $8.0 per million. mimo-v2.6-pro scores 46.3 and costs $0.5. Sixteen times less for 11% less index.

On coding it flips. mimo-v2.5 scores 60.2 on the coding index at $0.2 per million, and muse-spark-1.2-contributor scores 58.6 at $0.1. Those are models I would never have considered opening without seeing those numbers side by side.

Speed: claude-haiku-5-5 runs at 238.9 tok/s and deepseek-v4.1-flash at 216.1. But look at the first one's TTFT: 285.8 seconds. That's not time to first token, it's an artifact of the test (queues, rate limits, whatever happened that day). TTFT from the API has to be read with tongs.

And price. OpenCode's price doesn't come from Artificial Analysis: it comes from models.dev, which is the source OpenCode uses for its catalog. Comparing the two, there are models where OpenCode charges you noticeably less than the public reference: mimo-v2.5 68% less, longcat-2.0 60% less, deepseek-v4.1-flash 50% less.

Zen is a different picture. There the top models run $20 per million (claude-fable-5-1, gpt-6-astra), and the quality/price ranking fills up with models that don't even show in Go.

Four Go models have no Artificial Analysis data: omen-alpha, hy4-preview, longcat-2.5-preview-free, and beam-free. They're previews and free models, so that's expected. In JSON they show up with matched: false, and in the human table you list them with --show-unmatched.

How it matches models¶

OpenCode IDs and Artificial Analysis slugs almost never match, so the matcher tries three things in order:

Exact slug. gpt-5.4 against gpt-5.4. Normalizing first: lowercase, dots to dashes, and everything non-alphanumeric stripped.

Substring. If one contains the other, it keeps the shortest slug, which is the most specific one. That's where things like gemini-4-argon-contributor → gemini-4-argon land.

Token set. For reordered names, like haiku-4-5 against 4-5-haiku.

It's pure heuristics, there's no hand-written equivalence table. It works well enough, but a badly matched model gives you believable, wrong numbers, which is the worst kind of error. When OpenCode adds new models, it's worth eyeballing the row before trusting it.

What it doesn't do¶

  • It doesn't tell you which model suits you. It just puts the numbers together and sorts them.
  • It doesn't check availability: if a model is down, it won't notice.
  • It keeps no history. Every run is a snapshot.
  • There's no manual equivalence table, so odd matches are possible.

Using the free Artificial Analysis API requires attribution, so: benchmarks come from Artificial Analysis and OpenCode pricing from models.dev.

Original source: github.com/pcaro/aa-opencode

entry.title: qemu-wasm: full virtual machines inside your browser
entry.summary: qemu-wasm ports QEMU to WebAssembly to boot a full x86_64 virtual machine inside the browser. trynix.dev runs any nixpkgs package from the last 13 years, and a GitHub Action boots a PR's build from a single link.
entry.content:
Every once in a while something reminds me how far browsers have come. Today: a full x86_64 virtual machine, booting inside a tab, with no server behind it.

qemu-wasm is a patched QEMU that runs in the browser. It's not a reimplementation or a toy: it's QEMU compiled to WebAssembly, with JIT binary translation (TCG) and multi-threading support. The same QEMU you use on your machine, running in a tab.

How it works¶

QEMU has several backends for running guest code. The fastest is TCG, which translates the guest binary to native machine code. Here the "host" is WebAssembly, so the project adds a TCG backend that translates QEMU's IR to Wasm.

WebAssembly doesn't let you jump to code generated in memory, so instead they lean on browser APIs (WebAssembly.Module and WebAssembly.Instance). Each translation block (TB) is compiled as a standalone Wasm module that imports memory and helper functions from the main QEMU module.

The problem: compiling every block to Wasm is expensive, and browsers can't handle creating thousands of modules. So the solution is hybrid. Cold blocks are interpreted (TCI, the slow interpreter) and only blocks that run many times (~1000) get compiled to Wasm.

It's experimental software, but it works. There's a demo with x86_64, aarch64 (it even emulates a Raspberry Pi), and riscv64 guests. And part of this is being upstreamed into QEMU: the interpreter mode (TCI) for 32-bit guests already landed in QEMU 10.1, and the rest is still under discussion.

The use case that blew my mind: trynix.dev¶

Knowing the engine is fine, but the part I find brutal is the use Farid Zakaria gave it: trynix.dev.

The idea: boot an x86_64 Linux VM in your tab and give it a Nix store as its filesystem. The result is that you can run any nixpkgs package from the last 13 years — over 310,000 versions — without installing anything on your machine.

And they're URL-addressable. Try this:

https://trynix.dev/?pkg=python3%403.6.2

Click Boot and you get an interactive shell against a virtual machine running Python 3.6.2 from 2017. Nothing runs on a server: the page is static, the kernel is WebAssembly, and the package closure downloads from cache.nixos.org (which serves access-control-allow-origin: *, the thing that makes all this possible).

You can even boot two versions of hello at once without them clashing, because in Nix each binary references its dependencies by absolute path:

https://trynix.dev/?pkg=hello@2.10&pkg=hello@2.12.2

To make it feel instant, the site pre-fetches the engine and a VM snapshot in the background, and never boots from scratch: it resumes a machine that was booted once with the native QEMU and paused right before mounting the store.

The GitHub Action: review a PR by booting it¶

The most practical part is trynix-preview, a GitHub Action that comments on every pull request with a link to boot the PR's build in the browser. No servers, no SSH, no cloning, no building. Just a link.

# Set up Cachix as our Nix cache.
- uses: cachix/cachix-action@v17
  with:
    name: sqlelf
    authToken: ${{ secrets.CACHIX_AUTH_TOKEN }}
# Build the PR's code and push it to the cache.
- run: nix build .#default
- uses: fzakaria/trynix@v1
  with:
    cache: https://sqlelf.cachix.org
    publicKey: sqlelf.cachix.org-1:MLnjolA9AsKscTOJKDSA+ZAcgIK8BwZA574j4+Cs2bg=
    attrs: .#default

Two caveats: the action builds and caches nothing — you need to have filled the cache yourself — and since the workflow runs on fork PRs, use a segregated cache and allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true.

Limitations¶

It's not all magic:

  • Large binaries are slow: they can take 1-2 minutes to run. There's a benchmark page with data.
  • The whole closure has to fit in tab memory (~1.5 GiB cap, and WebAssembly limits it to 4 GiB since it's a 32-bit address space).
  • The first run of a binary is slow because it has to translate from x86_64 to Wasm; subsequent runs are faster because it's cached in memory.

Still, as a workflow for small and medium binaries it's impressive. "Does this fix the bug?" stops being a thought experiment.

Original source: Simon Willison - Any Nix package, live in your browser

entry.title: ku: navigate Kubernetes from the terminal like a pro
entry.summary: ku is a fast, keyboard-driven Kubernetes TUI inspired by k9s and lazygit. Read-only by default, with a cluster cockpit, logs, pod shells, port-forwarding, and object editing.
entry.content:
I'm back working with Kubernetes. I have a locally deployed microsite architecture — several namespaces, deployments, services, ingresses — and needed a fast way to navigate everything without constantly running kubectl get and kubectl describe by hand. kubectl muscle memory is fine, but to move through a cluster fluently you need to see the whole picture.

I went to GitHub and found ku, a Kubernetes TUI by a Norwegian developer. It's fast, keyboard-only, and clearly inspired by k9s, Lens, and lazygit. I liked it from the first ku.

Installation¶

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bjarneo/ku/main/install.sh | sh

Or with Go:

go install github.com/bjarneo/ku@latest

What sold me¶

  • Read-only by default. You start up and can't break anything. To edit, delete, or scale you have to enable edit mode with Shift+E. The header shows a green ● READ-ONLY or red ● EDIT chip so you always know what mode you're in. For those of us with butterfingers, this is peace of mind.

  • Cockpit on launch. A cluster overview: server version, node status, live CPU and memory gauges, pods by phase, ready deployments, and recent warnings (deduplicated, with recurrence count). Auto-refreshes every few seconds.

  • Tables with the right columns. Uses the same Table API representation as kubectl get, so columns are exactly what you expect for every resource. CRDs work too. Cells have semantic coloring: green for healthy, yellow for transient, red for broken. The sorted column shows its direction.

  • lazygit-style layout: left panel with resource navigation, Tab to switch panes, bottom status bar showing only the keys relevant to your current selection.

  • Curated summaries. Enter on an object opens a type-specific summary: pods show live usage, health, requests/limits; services, ingresses, configmaps, and secrets get purpose-built views. d or y opens the full YAML with syntax highlighting.

  • Logs with follow. l on a pod streams logs. Filter with regex, copy lines, switch between current and previous instance, and toggle auto-scroll. All inside the TUI.

  • Shell into pods and nodes. s on a pod opens an interactive shell (bash or sh) in an overlay with a virtual terminal. On a node, it spins up a privileged debug pod with chroot /host. Ctrl+\ detaches.

  • Service port-forwarding. p on a Service and pick the port. Map 8080:http or 18080:80. Active forwards show in the header and you manage them from the command palette.

  • Equivalent kubectl command. C shows the kubectl command that replicates the current view. Great for learning or copying to a script.

  • Built-in Kubernetes docs. O opens the upstream docs for the selected resource in your browser.

  • Customizable sidebar. ku config init generates ~/.config/ku/config.yaml where you can add CRDs to the sidebar. Supports group-qualified resources (scaledobjects.keda.sh, certificates.cert-manager.io).

  • Developer mode. ku --dev hides cluster admin resources (nodes, PVs, namespaces, events) and disables node operations. For when you only manage your own apps.

  • Remembers context and namespace. Persists them in ~/.config/ku/state.json between sessions.

What's missing (for now)¶

  • No dependency graph or topology view.
  • Port-forward is Services only, not individual pods.
  • No Helm integration.

It's a young project (~500 stars, ~100 commits) but very well thought out. Using it feels like a tool that understands how you work with Kubernetes and removes friction at every step. For my current setup — a microsite architecture with multiple namespaces — it lets me jump between resources, follow logs, and check cluster health without leaving the terminal.

Original source: github.com/bjarneo/ku

entry.title: AgentsView: local analytics for your coding agents
entry.summary: AgentsView is an open-source tool that indexes sessions from 20+ coding agents into a local SQLite database, providing analytics dashboards, cost tracking, and full-text search without sending data off your machine.
entry.content:
If you use multiple coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Cursor...) you know the feeling of losing track of what you've spent, which tools you use most, or which project eats up most of your time. Each agent stores sessions in its own format and directory, and until now there was no unified way to see everything together.

AgentsView fixes this. It's an open-source tool (Go + Svelte 5, MIT) that indexes all your coding agent sessions into a local SQLite database and gives you analytics dashboards, cost tracking, and full-text search. No accounts, no telemetry, no data leaving your machine.

Installation¶

# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://agentsview.io/install.sh | bash

# Or via Homebrew (desktop app)
brew install --cask agentsview

Once installed, start the server and open the dashboard at http://127.0.0.1:8080:

agentsview serve

On first run it automatically discovers sessions from all agents installed on your machine.

What you get¶

  • Cost dashboard: daily spend by agent and model, priced via LiteLLM. It also accounts for cache tokens (both creation and read).
  • Activity heatmap: visualize your most productive days and hours.
  • Full-text search (FTS5): search across all your past session content. Perfect for recovering that command or solution you used weeks ago.
  • Session viewer: browse sessions one by one, export to HTML, or publish as a GitHub Gist.
  • Per-project stats: tokens used, most frequent tools, average session duration.
  • Live updates via SSE: if you have active sessions, the dashboard updates automatically.

CLI for costs¶

Beyond the web dashboard, it has a fast CLI that replaces ccusage:

# Daily cost summary (last 30 days)
agentsview usage daily

# Per-model breakdown
agentsview usage daily --breakdown

# Filter by agent and date range
agentsview usage daily --agent claude --since 2026-05-01

# JSON output for scripting
agentsview usage daily --json

Since data is already indexed in SQLite, queries are way faster than re-parsing session files every time.

Supported agents¶

AgentsView auto-discovers sessions from 20+ agents: Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Cursor, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, OpenHands, Qwen Code, Kimi, Warp, Forge, Zencoder, and many more. The full list is in the README.

PostgreSQL for teams¶

If you work in a team, you can sync data to a shared PostgreSQL instance:

agentsview pg push --watch   # continuous sync
agentsview pg serve           # serve UI from PostgreSQL

The PostgreSQL-mode UI is read-only, so anyone on the team can view dashboards without modifying data.

What it doesn't do¶

  • It doesn't send data to any external server. The only optional outbound traffic is an update check on startup (disabled with --no-update-check).
  • No account or login required.
  • It doesn't replace the agent itself. It's an analytics layer on top of what you already have.

AgentsView fills a real gap in the coding agent ecosystem: unified visibility into how and how much you use these tools. If you use more than one agent, it's worth installing.

entry.title: Detecting secrets in git with gitleaks
entry.summary: gitleaks scans git repositories for secrets, API keys, and leaked credentials. Install it in seconds with gah — it might save you from a very bad day.
entry.content:
gitleaks scans git repositories —including the full commit history— for secrets: API keys, passwords, AWS tokens, database credentials, and over 150 predefined patterns.

Installing with gah¶

The fastest way on Linux is with gah, a GitHub release asset downloader:

$ gah install gitleaks/gitleaks
Fetching release info for: gitleaks/gitleaks [latest]
Found release: v8.30.1
Downloading: gitleaks_8.30.1_linux_x64.tar.gz
############################################### 100.0%
Verifying digest sha256 551f6fc8... ...
Digest verification succeeded!
Extracting: gitleaks_8.30.1_linux_x64.tar.gz
Installing: gitleaks
Done!

Single binary, zero dependencies, ready in seconds.

Basic usage¶

To scan a local repo with full commit history:

$ gitleaks git --verbose -v /path/to/repo

It walks every commit and shows what secrets it found, in which file and at which line.

Some useful flags:

  • --no-banner: hides the ASCII banner at startup.
  • --exit-code 0: don't exit with error when leaks are found (handy for CI).
  • --config .gitleaks.toml: use a custom config with your own detection rules.
  • --gitleaks-ignore-path .: respects the .gitleaksignore file for false positives.
  • --redact: masks secrets in output (useful for public logs).

You can also scan standalone directories with gitleaks dir or pipe content through gitleaks stdin.

When to use it¶

  • Before making a repo public: scan the full history to make sure no keys slipped through.
  • In CI/CD: add it as a GitHub Actions step so the build fails if someone commits a secret.
  • Security audits: great for reviewing old repos that have been touched by many people.

Pre-commit hook¶

The most effective way to use it is as a pre-commit hook that automatically blocks any commit containing secrets:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

if [[ "${SKIP_GITLEAKS:-}" == "1" || "${SKIP_GITLEAKS:-}" == "true" ]]; then
  echo "Skipping gitleaks pre-commit scan because SKIP_GITLEAKS=${SKIP_GITLEAKS}." >&2
  exit 0
fi

if ! command -v gitleaks >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  cat >&2 <<'EOF'
gitleaks is required by this repository's pre-commit hook but was not found.
Install gitleaks, or set SKIP_GITLEAKS=1 for an intentional one-off bypass.
EOF
  exit 1
fi

echo "Running gitleaks on staged changes..." >&2
gitleaks protect --staged --source . --redact --no-banner

Save this as .githooks/pre-commit, make it executable (chmod +x), and configure git to use that directory:

git config core.hooksPath .githooks

From then on, every git commit will scan staged changes for secrets. Need to bypass it once? SKIP_GITLEAKS=1 git commit.

It's one of those tools you don't need until you really need it. And when that day comes, you'll be glad it's just a gah install away.

entry.title: Cleaning up npx's hidden cache
entry.summary: npx leaves a hidden package cache in ~/.npm/_npx/. Here's how to list what you've accumulated and clean it up.
entry.content:
You run npx howcode to try out a tool, it doesn't convince you, and you move on. Do this a few times and, without realizing it, you've got hundreds of megabytes sitting in a cache you didn't even know existed.

The problem¶

Every time you run npx <package>, npm downloads the package and stores it in ~/.npm/_npx/. This isn't like npm install — there's no package.json or node_modules you can inspect. It's an opaque cache that keeps growing without you noticing.

After playing around with a few tools, here's what I had:

$ npm cache npx ls
06d0829110b3b3f: skill
135b94ef511a5b29: pi-kanban
1bf0be162bc0d832: @mvanhorn/printing-press
483d2954a4c5190c: madge
69c381f8ad94b576: vitest
7439c0f00f94bc1a: snipgrapher
9126f0a380537b3d: howcode   # 237 MB for this one alone

The trap¶

Your first instinct is npm cache npx rm vitest howcode and call it a day. Not so fast:

$ npm cache npx rm vitest snipgrapher howcode
npm error code EUSAGE
npm error Invalid npx key vitest

npm cache npx rm only accepts the hex hash, not the package name. You need to copy the key from the first column:

$ npm cache npx rm 9126f0a380537b3d 7439c0f00f94bc1a 69c381f8ad94b576
Removing npx key at /home/pcaro/.npm/_npx/9126f0a380537b3d
Removing npx key at /home/pcaro/.npm/_npx/7439c0f00f94bc1a
Removing npx key at /home/pcaro/.npm/_npx/69c381f8ad94b576

If you want to nuke everything at once, npm cache clean wipes the entire npm cache (including npx's). More drastic, but faster.
